paragraphs.text:
ON THE MEETING OF THE LORD, AND ON THE THEOTOKOS

Paul is lofty in his understanding of heavenly things and raised high by his contempt for earthly things. He is the God-possessed mind and the Christ-moved tongue, the finest pen of the swift-writing scribe, which wrote out the doctrines of truth for the Church in a fair hand. He is the arrow forged by God in the hand of the Mighty One, which struck a mortal wound into the heart of the world-ruler of darkness. He is the lightning that flashed from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum, or rather to the ends of the earth. He is the clear and loud-sounding voice of the divine thunder in the mystical wheel of the Gospel, which has rolled over the whole inhabited world. He speaks as if from the inner sanctuaries of paradise itself, where he heard the unspeakable words with his own ears, or rather as if from the very throne of glory, high and lifted up, where he stands. He is preparing an honourable escort for this present holy feast of the Lord, to receive the King of glory. As if it were a most mystical senate, he arranges the people of the Church, the royal priesthood, in ranks, so to speak. He sets out the order of a seemly way of life with good measure and harmony, and he says: "Brothers, do not be children in your thinking; be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature." For in this way we shall become members of one body and partakers with the all-perfect and eternal God, whose festival we keep today. For our sake, in the last times, he became an infant according to the flesh, and from him comes every perfect gift. Even in his human condition he displayed, in a manner beyond nature, the perfection of virtue that is his by nature. And so the assembly of the Church will be for his honour and glory. In this way the prophetic word hints at his newly born bodily manifestation as God and sketches it with the marks of his godlike perfection. For it says: "Before the child knows good or evil, he refuses wickedness, to choose the good." This is the mark of the highest and

most perfect discernment, and truly of wisdom. To shape us after his likeness, the great apostle spoke the divinely inspired saying quoted above. In this way the divine making according to image and likeness is recognised in us by resemblance, and the surpassing holiness of the archetypal beauty is made known. When the armies under a king prepare a magnificent escort for him, those gathered to be his bodyguard ought to be decked in gold and chosen men, and they should display the imprint of his appearance as clearly as possible. In the same way we must be transformed by the renewal of our mind and put off the old man. As far as is possible for human beings, we must carry in ourselves the likeness of the divine image, and so go out to meet the saving and spiritual feasts. Then, as the prophet says, the fast of the fourth month, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh and the fast of the tenth will become gladness and good feasts for us. Here the fast is understood in a higher sense, as abstaining and refraining from every defilement of flesh and spirit. For the fourth and the fifth, and also the seventh and the tenth, signify everything that appears fleshly, is akin to the easily deceived senses, and is confined to the present life. By the four we learn the more bodily and flesh-loving way of life, since bodies are compounded of four elements. The name of the fifth hints at how easily we slip through the senses, since there are five of them. The seventh, as Solomon also shows, indicates the age of the lower order, which turns back on itself in cycles of seven. The tenth points to the purification of the senses of the inner man, which has been led away from external things. Then the eye of the mind will be single and clear, so that the whole body may be full of light, as the holy [?] says. [?] of exultation and gladness, which the great David prays to be made to hear. Its power of taste must be trained in the goodness of the Lord, as the psalmist among the prophets exclaims. Its sense of smell must be set in the perception of the fragrance of Christ, which the divine Paul breathed out. And with the inner hands of discernment it must handle the Word of life, as the son of thunder declared. When the spiritual senses are exercised in these things, and when we abstain from their opposites and keep ourselves apart from them, this naturally produces the fast that God praises. In this way we succeed in being

infants in evil, but mature in the wisdom that is according to God. The greatness of mind of the apostolic and prophetic teachings flows together from the fountains of the Spirit. It waters us and fills the river of God with mystical waters, and so it knows how to gladden with the rushing streams of this river the heavenly city of God, which is made up of the powers above the world. We heard the psalmody cry this out. For the holy assembly of the spirits above rejoices greatly at the salvation of human beings. Heavenly beings are accustomed to celebrate together with those on earth, welcoming the angelic way of life of those who live here. This our God, whom the prophet foretold, was seen on earth and lived among men. When the angels saw the blessedness above being planted on earth, they cried, "Glory to God in the highest," and announced peace on earth, since divine good pleasure had come to be among men. In the same way, the blessed choirs of holy angels, who take pride in a divine liturgy that is select, truly pure and single-minded, will see in us the marks of true holiness. They will not cast us out but will take us along as partners in their untainted gladness. By contrast, the word of the Gospel parable shut out from the divine wedding the man dressed in a filthy garment. At the archetypal time of the present feast, so to speak, he who was in the form of God took the form of a servant and became mediator between God and men. To fulfil the prescription of the Law, the eternal Word, an infant of forty days, went to the temple with the mother who bore him and with the sacrifice that had been prescribed. Then the ranks of the bodiless powers bowed their necks like servants and invisibly prepared an escort fit for God. They praised the ocean of ineffable wisdom as divine. They welcomed the passing beyond the more obvious ordinance of the letter of the Law as the revelation of the mystery hidden in God, who created all things. As we celebrate its memory today, let us delight in spiritual contemplations like the bodiless minds. By glorifying the greatness of the divine wonders, we shall share in their dignity. We will not let the shadow of the Law darken the eye of the soul. Rather, in the words of the most wise Paul, with unveiled face we will behold the glory of the Lord as in a mirror. The Law says that every male that opens the womb is to be consecrated. It says that a woman who has just given birth and become the mother of a male child must be purified for forty days after the birth,

and then go to the sanctuary of God with a specific, clearly defined sacrifice. There are those who keep the veil over their heart when the Old Testament is read. Let them think, childishly, that they fulfil this legislation by the same sacrifices offered year by year (sacrifices which, if I may say so, can never perfect those who draw near). But when we turned to God, that veil was taken away from us. We have believed that the great mystery of godliness was revealed once for all at the end of the age, to put away sin by his sacrifice. So we must contemplate the mystery of the present festival in a way worthy of the divine light of truth, by the torchlight of the Spirit. We will approach the contemplation from a little further back. First, it is timely to note that, as the course of our inquiry will show, the decree of the Law quoted above is seen to be fulfilled definitively in the incarnate God alone, and in no one else. He alone was conceived ineffably and carried in the womb beyond all telling. He alone opened the virginal womb, which had not been opened before by marriage, and he kept the seals of virginity unbroken even after his marvellous going forth. He alone is believed to be male in the spiritual sense, since he brought on himself nothing of effeminate sin. For this reason he is also fittingly called truly holy. Gabriel brought the good news of the life-giving birth to the Theotokos as if he were recalling the legislation laid down in advance about this birth, which looked to him alone. He said: "Therefore the holy one who is born will be called Son of God." The name "holy" properly belongs to the one who opened the virgin womb by divine wonder-working. Concerning the other firstborn, the precision of the Gospel stooped down and searched the depths of the Law, and it declared that they "shall be called holy." They received this name by lot through their dedication to God. But concerning the firstborn of all creation, the angel called the one being born "Holy" because he properly is holy. As soon as he was born he showed true holiness by rejecting evil and choosing the good, as the prophet says. But we must put out again onto the sea of contemplation, as the divine voice commands the lawgiver. The grace of the Spirit goes before the godly camp of the Church with the brightness of the Scriptures, as in the pillar of fire and cloud. Let us take the rod of power sent from Zion above, as the psalmist says, by which enemies are mastered. Then, having crossed the sea of the letter,

which is divided this way and that as the meanings are clearly passed through, we may escape the Egyptian mind of those who disobey grace, while the stream of truth overwhelms them. They are eager to block our road to the spiritual promised land of the Gospel. They want us to stay in the iron furnace of the letter, for that is what Egypt is called, slaving at clay and brickmaking, that is, at the bodily observances of the Law. So, when the God of all had already decreed the plague against the firstborn of Egypt, he said to Moses in Egypt: "Consecrate to me every firstborn, the first-produced that opens every womb among the sons of Israel, both man and beast." This divine legislation was stated briefly, and the blessed Moses, as if unfolding it, declares it in his address to the people: "And when the Lord your God brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to you and to your fathers, 'And I will give it to you,' you shall set apart to the Lord everything that opens the womb, the males. And everything that opens the womb from the herds [?] or among your cattle, whatever you have, the males belong to the Lord. Everything that opens the womb of a donkey you shall exchange for a sheep; and if you do not exchange it, you shall redeem it. And every firstborn of your sons you shall redeem" — that is, you shall pay a ransom for him. The divine oracle makes this clear in the book of Numbers, speaking to the one who had taken up the high priesthood: "Everything that opens the womb of all flesh, which they offer to the Lord, both man and beast, shall be yours. But the firstborn of men shall surely be redeemed with a ransom, and the firstborn of unclean beasts you shall redeem. And its redemption: from a month old you shall redeem it, at a valuation of five shekels of silver, according to the holy shekel. But the firstborn of calves, the firstborn of sheep and of goats you shall not redeem, for they are holy, and their blood you shall pour out at the altar." So the divine voice has already yoked the firstborn of Israel together with the unclean beasts and counted them with them. They did not have true purity and holiness in the worship of the Law, even if the allotment of the legislation was thought to consecrate them. In the same way as for the beasts rejected from God's sacrifice, the Law decreed among them that a ransom be paid for human beings. For the rather irrational condition of the Jews was unworthy to offer the rational worship and to be brought to the most mystical altar of the New Covenant as a spiritual whole burnt offering. As ransoms it was accustomed to offer things suited to itself, the blood sacrifices of the Law (which the prophet Isaiah, speaking in the person of God, declares were never even required from their hands). The aim of the lawgiver plainly looked to a spiritual fulfilment. But the things brought for sacrifice, whose blood

was by custom poured out at the altar, were expressly named "holy." In this, too, the truth was clearly sketched beforehand in the type. For our Lord Jesus Christ brought himself to God the Father as a sacrifice and offering, a fragrant aroma, and he alone properly and truly is holy and is called so. But perhaps the unbelieving Jew will say this: the firstborn of the beasts he counts unclean cannot be brought in the sacrifice of the Law, so they are usually exchanged for a ransom. Likewise, human firstborn are not slaughtered as sacrifices (for that would be unseemly and foreign to divine legislation), so it is reasonable that they are consecrated by paying a ransom in exchange. But let him consider, if the veil lying over the eyes of their souls does not hinder him, that the sacred Scripture had already taught in another law that the Levites were taken for dedication in place of the firstborn. In Numbers it says, word for word: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Behold, I have taken the Levites from among the sons of Israel in place of every firstborn that opens the womb among the sons of Israel. They shall be their ransom, and the Levites shall be mine. For every firstborn is mine; I consecrated it in Israel on the day I struck every firstborn in Egypt." Then the Law sets out the exactness of the exchange: "The Lord said to Moses: Number every firstborn male of the sons of Israel from a month old and upward, and take the number of their names. And you shall take the Levites for me in place of all the firstborn of the sons of Israel." Then, when the firstborn were counted against the number of the Levites and found to exceed it, it says: "The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take the ransom for those in excess of the Levites from the firstborn of the sons of Israel, and you shall take five shekels a head, according to the holy didrachm." According to the sacred Scripture, then, the Levites are the ransom of the firstborn of the sons of Israel, as the exact count shows, since a fixed weight was paid by law for those who exceeded their number. If so, on what reasoning did the Law declare that a ransom be paid for each of the firstborn? In the case of beasts unacceptable for sacrifice, the Law says either that they are to be exchanged or that a ransom is to be paid for them. In the case of human beings, however, we learn both that a ransom is paid and that the exchange had already been made through the Levites. This seems inconsistent even with the letter of the Law itself, as the legislation about beasts shows and as the very nature of the matter suggests. For after the Levites had been allotted to the service of God in place of the firstborn,

it is still prescribed that a ransom be paid for them. It is therefore clear that the Levites were not of equal worth or acceptable as a ransom. If that is so, the redemption paid in silver is far more unworthy, just as all irrational and insensible nature is less honourable than human nature. But since, as the prophet says, they have shut their eyes and cannot see what follows from this, will they be able to hear the most wise Micah crying out? I do not think so, for their ears are also hard of hearing. Nevertheless, let this blessed prophet come and cry out loudly. By the prophetic spirit he hints in advance that the Jewish firstborn will be rejected, just like the offering of bodily sacrifices. For he says: "With what shall I come upon the Lord and lay hold of my God most high? Shall I come upon him with yearling calves? Will the Lord accept thousands of rams, or tens of thousands of fat [?] goats? Shall I give my firstborn for ungodliness, the fruit of my womb for my sins?" Let those whose hearts are fat hear it, as the prophet charged against them: the blessed Micah called the firstborn of Israel according to the flesh "firstborn of ungodliness." How then have they supposed these to be holy, when the prophetic word called them firstborn of ungodliness? Let those truly stammering tongues, which cannot speak the truth plainly, tell us how the prophet, speaking in the Holy Spirit, dared to call these the fruit of ungodliness. And why does the account of their redemption not appear even and consistent with itself, if we go by the surface sense of the letter? Yet we understand and believe the Law to be holy and spiritual. You see the axles of the Jewish chariots bound fast, just as the chariots of the Egyptians once were at the waters of the Red Sea. But instead of a rod, let the power and help of Christ, the true lawgiver and King of glory, be stretched out over the sea of the discourse. Let it lead his people on a straight road of higher meaning and contemplation, so that they may go to a city of habitation, the city of knowledge and truth. And let the irresistible [?] of divine glory cover the adversaries. The whole earth is full of this glory, so that it knows the Lord, as Scripture says, as abundant water covers the seas. On the one hand, as soon as he was born according to the flesh, the incarnate God put to death and destroyed the devil's firstborn offspring, that is, sin. He passed the sentence of condemnation on evil in himself and brought about its complete destruction in himself,

and he filled the opposing powers with lamentation. He took from them, as if they were vessels, the Magi who came from the east. By their worship and their recognition of his lordship they became useful vessels for the Master, to help build the Church, the truly God-made tabernacle which the Lord pitched, and not man. On the other hand, just as he once redeemed Israel from clay and brickmaking, so now he has redeemed the human race in himself from earthly-mindedness. He has made it flee Egypt, that is, the hateful and gloomy prison of Hades. He consecrates to God the Father not only the firstborn of human beings but now the whole human race as well. He does this through the firstfruits of our lump in him, that is, through the flesh he took from us, endowed with a rational soul. In this way he leavens, as it were, the whole compound of human nature for sanctification. "If the firstfruits are holy, so is the lump," I too might fittingly say now, with the divine Apostle. Of old, the word of the lawgiver offered to God, as a type, the tribe that had been allotted the priesthood in place of the firstfruits of the firstborn. So now, in the bright stamp of the truth, we know that the high priest and apostle of our confession was offered bodily to God the Father in place of the humanity sanctified to him through faith. He is holy, innocent and undefiled, separated from every sinful way [?] and thought. And this offering is far greater. In the shadow of the Law the firstborn were found to outnumber the Levites. But we do not see the whole of humanity exceeding or outweighing, in terms of holiness, the one who gave himself as a ransom for many. Rather, humanity falls far behind him, since beyond all dispute the lesser is blessed by the greater. Then the dignity of the Levitical priesthood was granted to the one nation of Israel alone, and the Levites are attested to be the ransom only for the firstborn among them. But Christ came as high priest of the good things to come, as the all-wise Paul says, not according to the order of Aaron but according to the order of Melchizedek, as the divine oracle foretold. The priesthood was changed because he is of another tribe (for it is evident that our Lord Jesus Christ sprang from Judah), and through this he also brought about a change of the law. He transferred us from the shadow of the Law to the Gospel of the kingdom of heaven, just as he transferred the dignity of the priesthood from the Levitical tribe to the royal tribe. Because he is like Melchizedek, according to his order, he offered himself to the Father as a ransom not for Israel alone but for all the nations, and he became high priest of the confession of all people. For Melchizedek too is known to belong to the gentile [?] portion and is found to stand outside [?] the race of Abraham. But the redemption of five didrachms according to the Law

[?] …the valuation paid for each of the firstborn conveys in a figure that each of us must consecrate every sense to God, together with what belongs to it, and bring it to the Creator pure and free of every improper pleasure, as a holy ransom, and [?]

Today we celebrate the remembrance of this sacred rite. This spiritual unfolding of the mystery has brought together the present holy festival, at which the Saviour was outwardly presented according to the law. But inwardly and spiritually, by presenting to the Father the firstfruits of our common dough, he showed the whole of it to be holy and fit to be brought to God. This is what the law had long been in labour with, and this is what the legislation about the firstborn looked toward, as did the exchange of the Levites and the valuation of the two-drachma pieces. So the grace of the Spirit has brought us across the sea of the holy Scriptures. But let us also see our adversaries shut in and destroyed. The whole legislation about the Levites and the firstborn has already been made clear to us above. But just as the great Moses encouraged the people and assured them that they would never see the Egyptians again, so I too am now moved to bring God's own people the good news that we shall no longer see the bodily army of shadowy worship. For after the great High Priest has appeared, where is the ministry of the Levites? After the ransom that cleanses the world, where is the valuation of the firstborn? Where is all the rest of the exactness of the legal rite? Do you not see that while the night of ignorance held all things, the worship under the law gave a dim and limited light, like the stars? But when the sun of righteousness rose, and the dawn from on high appeared, and the day of salvation shone forth, the torchlight of the legal ordinances vanished in the surpassing light [?] overcome by grace. Has not that renowned temple [?] been levelled to the ground like the captains and the chariots, along with all the pride and arrogance of the high priests over it? Has not their whole legal order been flooded and thrown into confusion? Has not the exactness of Jewish customs utterly perished? For where could they offer the sacrifices for women who have just given birth, now that the chosen place has fallen, when it was clearly laid down that they may not offer sacrifices anywhere else? Where is the priestly vestment, the priestly rank, and all the rest? But we should not go through each thing in turn, lest we [?] the eye of the soul by constant contact with corpses and the sight of them. So let us leave those people lying dead beside

the [?] water of the letter of the law. As for us, let us sing the hymn of victory to the God who loves humankind. Fed with the truly heavenly food, and given drink from the stream of the true rock, let us come to Horeb, the mountain of God, that is, to the lofty teaching of the Gospel. There, at the sound of the divine trumpets, let us turn our inner hearing to the words of blessed Luke, who cries out the mystagogy of the Spirit as if from a holy sanctuary: "And when the days of their purification were fulfilled, the parents brought the child Jesus up to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord, 'Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord,' and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon, and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel. The Holy Spirit was upon him, and it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ in the flesh. And he came in the Spirit into the temple." What does "waiting for the consolation of Israel" mean? It means awaiting the manifestation of the truth, and the passing over of the people of Israel to it from the shadow of the law. Released from being under the elements of the world, they would be taught their first lessons in the school of truth and brought to the perfection that belongs to it. No one could claim that the Jews were in distress or held in some kind of captivity, and that he was awaiting their restoration and their return to good cheer and their former state. All their ancient customs were then in good order: the temple was standing, the sacrifices in it were being offered, and every other part of the way of life peculiar to their nation was preserved. Someone may object that they were under the Romans, and that Herod, a foreigner by race, had been made king of Judea. Let such a person know that the way of life under the law was not harmed at all by Israel being ruled by a foreigner, so as to make the righteous old man await consolation about that. Indeed, Israel often came under foreign rule at various times, just as a father hands a rebellious son over to a strict tutor to be disciplined. This is shown by the people's very long stay in Egypt, and by the prophet Jeremiah, who in the days of King Zedekiah, by divine command, told the king and the people under him to submit to the sceptre of Nebuchadnezzar and go over to the Chaldeans.

It was not unreasonable that these people, who deserved a harsher regime, should be made subject to a foreign sceptre. But God's long-suffering has also shown some of the righteous, "of whom the world was not worthy," to use Paul's words, not as rulers but as ruled by barbarous and godless men, so that the proven quality of their piety would shine out clearly. Abraham shows this: he went down to Egypt, had his wife taken from him by Pharaoh, and lived as a sojourner in the land promised to him. So do his son and grandson, I mean Isaac and Jacob, and again Jacob's most chaste son Joseph, who became a slave and was condemned to live in prison. So the wise Simeon was not awaiting a consolation of Israel that meant worldly glory and boasting, but the true one: the passing over to the beauty of the truth. Since it had been revealed to him that before he departed this life he would see the Lord's Christ appear, he awaited the people's consolation in a spiritual sense. So he came in the Spirit into the temple, "and when the parents brought in the child Jesus to do for him according to the custom of the law, he took him in his arms and blessed God and said: 'Now, Master, you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and the glory of your people Israel.'" O truly blessed, thrice-blessed old man! How blessed was that truly holy entry of yours into the temple, by which you ran toward your exit from life! How blessed were the eyes of your soul and of your body together! The eyes of your body came to perceive the visible appearance of God. The eyes of your soul did not look only at what was seen; lit by the very light of the Spirit, they recognised God the Word in the body and knew the divine salvation prepared before the face of all peoples. How blessed were your hands, which touched the Word of life! How blessed was your tongue, which proclaimed the revelation of the life-giving light! But why do I hurry to fit a separate praise to each of your members, when the evangelist has already taught that you are wholly praiseworthy and blessed, as one possessed by the Holy Spirit? Come then, blessed Father, and by the voice of the Spirit sounding within you, teach us, the children and nurslings of the Church, the hidden treasure contained in your few words as in earthen vessels. For the divine word sends us to you and to those like you, who are adorned with the grey hair of wisdom from above, who are truly elders and bear the name of Fathers of the Church, to learn the teachings of salvation. It says: "Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will speak to you."

May the power of the Spirit that once moved his tongue to speak of God give us too a word now, as we open our mouth. "Now, Master," he says, "you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word." Ever since Christ became man, abolished sin, the maker of war, and reconciled us to the Father, the saints depart in peace. Great David foretold this prophetically when he said, "In peace I will lie down and sleep," hinting not at the present but at what was to come with Christ's coming. And since such a hope, I mean the hope of peaceful sleep in Christ, had been settled in the saints by the Spirit in one way alone, he says, "For you alone, Lord, have made me dwell in hope." But the blessed old man Simeon, seeing that the time had now arrived, says, "Now, Master, you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word," showing that the divine promise was now present. "For my eyes have seen your salvation," he says, "which you have prepared before the face of all peoples," that is, the salvation that came through Christ to the whole world, and not to Israel alone. How then, when the text has testified above that he was waiting for the consolation of Israel, does he now proclaim that God's salvation has appeared before all peoples? Because he knew by the Spirit that the consolation of Israel would come at the time when salvation had also been prepared for all peoples. See how precise the divine inspiration is. "A light," he says, "for revelation to the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel." Here he speaks in agreement with the great Paul when Paul gives his account of Israel: "When the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved." So Simeon too puts the calling of the Gentiles first and, in keeping with the prophecy, keeps the conversion of all Israel for last, even though the remnant has already been saved through those from among the Jews who have already hastened to grace. Consider with me also how exactly the lofty ideas are expressed. By saying "for revelation to the Gentiles" he gives us to understand that the divine salvation was revealed to people who had no gleam of the knowledge of God, as if they were in utter darkness and complete gloom. That was the state of the Gentiles before Christ's coming, as blessed Isaiah too declared when he brought good news to the people sitting in darkness and said that they had seen a great light. But Israel, though only to a limited degree, was still enlightened by the law of types and figures. So he did not speak of light in Israel's case, but foretold that it would receive glory, recalling an ancient story. Long ago the wonderful Moses spoke with God and his face was glorified. In the same way, they too, having drawn near through faith to the divine light of the incarnation and been lit up by the power of the Spirit, will appear in glory. They will lay aside the old veil and be transformed into the same image, "from glory to glory," as the Apostle says, "as by the Lord, the Spirit."

The godly Simeon said that the Lord was set for the fall and rising of many in Israel. Because this meaning agrees with the prophetic announcements, it shows that one and the same God and Lawgiver spoke both in the prophets and in the New Testament. For the prophetic word declared that the stone of stumbling and rock of offence would be the reason why those who believe in him will not be put to shame. So he is a fall for those who stumble in unbelief over the lowliness of the flesh, but a rising for those who have recognised how firm the divine plan of salvation is. And when he says that a sword would pierce the soul of the Mother of God herself, he plainly prophesies the suffering of the cross. From the wondrous conception itself up to the time of the passion, all that was said and done concerning him in a manner worthy of God formed, as it were, one undivided body, and from it the Mother of God held a lofty and godlike view of him. So we will consider that she suffered a kind of cutting in the shame of the crucifixion, although the miracle of the resurrection healed the wound completely. Yet he does not indicate that she alone would be gripped by such suffering. He foretells that the thoughts of many hearts would be revealed as doubts and divisions, so that the Virgin Mother of God might not be shaken by the differing opinions about him. The prophetess Anna, because of her old age, speaks in a feeble and barely audible voice, and the lofty Gospel does not report her words word for word. So let us first learn from the evangelist who she was and where she came from, and on what grounds and when she was attending the temple, and then let us investigate the meaning of what she said. Blessed Luke says: "There was Anna the prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in many days, having lived with a husband seven years after her virginity, and she was a widow of about eighty-four years. She did not depart from the temple, with fastings and [?]"

[?] having been taught, as the divine Apostle says, to speak mysteries in the Spirit. As far as we are able, we say that there were other women at that time who shared this blessed woman's name and devoted themselves to the same sacred pursuits as she did, persevering in fasts and prayers. So, to make clear which person she was, he added what was distinctive about her by mentioning her father and her tribe. He also crowned her with great praises, which certainly give credibility among the hearers to what she said about the Lord. But since, as has been said, old age had taken away the carrying power and strength of her voice, let us place the ear of our mind close to her mouth, as it were, by investigating the present subject, and see what she too was saying to those who were waiting for redemption in Jerusalem. Following the logic of the thought, she was speaking about the Lord from the words of the prophets. For those to whom, the Gospel says, she spoke these things had surely learned to await redemption from the divine oracles given in the prophets. Surely the word of the great Isaiah was close at hand for her to describe the mystery: "A child has been born to us, a son has also been given to us, whose rule has come upon his shoulder," and "his name is called the Angel of Great Counsel." And again: "Shine, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you." Great David too was brought forward: "Mercy and truth have met, righteousness and peace have kissed"; and "All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God." And pointing to him: "His name endures before the sun, and in him all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed. All the nations shall call him blessed, and they shall serve him and worship him"; and "The Lord has made known his salvation to the sons of Israel." And again the honoured, angel-like voice of wise Malachi: "Behold, I will send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before your face; and suddenly the Lord will come to his temple, and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire." With other mystical flowers of prophetic oracles, gathered from here and there, she wove her blessed crown of praise to God, though with a hand still weak and trembling, being advanced in many days. For at that time her hearers could hardly take in an account of lofty ideas about the Lord. Even after so great a display of signs and so full a proclamation of divine mysteries, Christ, the steward of the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, said to his own disciples: "I have many things to tell you, but you cannot bear them now." All the same, the aged prophetess spoke her word about the Lord, even if dimly, as of the law

Come, let us rejoice in the Lord, let us shout aloud to God our Saviour. Let us say, "How awesome are your works, O Lord! In the greatness of your power your enemies have lied to you," for they deliberately shut their eyes to your divine light that appeared to the world. Let us come before his face with thanksgiving, and shout aloud to him with psalms. Let us continually offer God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name, and let us not forget to do good and to share, for God is pleased with such sacrifices. Then we will wash away the filth of sin, and our spiritual youth will be renewed like the eagle's, as was that of the blessed old man Simeon. Then we too may run toward our departure from life peacefully and joyfully, in good confidence and saving hope. We will not leave this present life in shame and fear, unwilling as it were, like people with wicked deeds on their conscience, who find the king's visit unpleasant and hateful. Let us imitate the intense and unflagging devotion of blessed Anna in fasts and prayers. Let us not prove worse than a woman, and a woman who lived under the shadow of the law at that, when excellence in these things was rare. We are lit by the light of grace, helped by a hope that is clear and more distinct, and strengthened by the might of the Spirit. So let us not be separated from the sacred teachings, from which a saving disposition is usually born in souls, just as she too is attested to have never left the temple. Let us not let our thoughts wander from the fear of God. Rather, by it and in it, let us nail down our flesh and our thoughts, as the prophet prays. Let us hear the great Paul teaching: "I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ." Let us not break our covenant with him by joining ourselves to the corrupter of our life through doing his will. In this too let us imitate the chastity of the prophetess and her single marriage. As far as you readily can, do not fall short in imitating her, you who have been released from your one marriage, and if you can [?]

[?] do not enter a second marriage. For Paul assures you that in this way you will be more blessed. Let us too bring to the altar on high the purity of soul and body, like a pair of turtledoves, or, like two young pigeons, our care for what is good not only in the sight of the Lord but also in the sight of men. Then we too, having fulfilled everything spiritually according to the divine law, advancing in wisdom and grace, reaching the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, being perfected in the inner man and becoming a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, may return to our true homeland, the heavenly Jerusalem. There may we be counted worthy to enjoy blessed and unending gladness and the kingdom in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and might with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages.
